items_missed: No agenda statement and no 'sound good?' confirmation — jumped straight from the apology for the late callback into asking for zip codes

Save Your Ass prep speech entirely absent — no prep-equals-shorter-move framing, no consolidation examples (toys, drawers, photos off walls), no 'take a carload' tip, no sense-check close. Highest-value miss on a call where the customer is self-packing with six days to move day
On-Time Guarantee not pitched — said 'a strict punctuality policy' but never explained that Einstein starts discounting immediately if the window is missed
No 'no hidden fees' pitch — never said no credit card fees, no transportation fees, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees
What's-included list was thin: only moving blankets and disassembly/reassembly; skipped gas, truck, taxes, tools, bands
Never asked about additional rooms (garage, storage unit, balcony/patio)
Never asked about storage stops or additional stops
Never asked the moving-stressor question ('anything you're particularly worried about with this move?')
No 'does that make sense?' sense-check after the clock/proration explanation — the customer volunteered 'that makes sense' on his own
Never mentioned the truck count in the estimate (movers only)
Never mentioned the bolded detail list at the top of the confirmation email or framed the reply-back as verifying/correcting details — only asked for the two street addresses
Never asked 'any other questions before I let you go?' — the customer had to prompt with 'is there anything else we need to discuss'
top_strength: The insurance explanation was the best moment on the call — when Jonathan asked him to repeat the $2,000 piece, Alex contrasted it against the 60-cent-per-pound state baseline, tied it to a concrete high-value item the customer actually owns (the TV and the China cabinet), and framed it as 'if we drop the ball' rather than as a sales feature. He also handled the customer's seven-minute break window well: he named the time constraint out loud, compressed the pricing walkthrough, and quoted both a 3.5-hour and a 4-hour scenario so Jonathan could see the realistic top end.
coaching_note: This call booked, so it feels like a win — but Alex left the entire Save Your Ass prep speech on the table on the one call where it mattered most: Jonathan is packing himself, moving Sunday, and going down and up stairs at both ends. Two minutes on consolidating loose items into boxes, clearing the drawers, taking photos off walls, and 'take a carload of the small stuff yourself' is the difference between the 3.5-hour quote and the 4-hour quote he just gave. Alex should build the habit of running Save Your Ass immediately after the estimate range, every time — it protects estimate accuracy, not just the customer's bill. Second, when he compresses for time, the differentiators are what get cut: Meet Your Mover, the real On-Time Guarantee (not just 'strict punctuality policy'), and the no-hidden-fees list all disappeared. Those three should be a fixed 30-second block that never gets dropped.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently polite, used Jonathan's name five-plus times, opened with an apology for the late callback and closed warmly — but the language was transactional and filler-heavy ('Okay. Okay. Perfect. Good deal.') with no humor, empathy statements, or rapport moment beyond the task.
